verdict.rationale: Both changes replace the linear `findIndex` scan with a normalized-email → index Map. Both keep first-occurrence merge semantics and arrival order, and both add a test pinning the duplicate-existing-entries behavior. B adds a 1-second wall-clock assertion over 80k generated contacts, which can fail on slow CI machines. A deliberately left that test out and explained why. B's code reads slightly cleaner, but the possibly flaky test in the permanent suite tips it toward A.
a_issues: The `remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)` line relies on push's return value, which is a bit too clever.
New contacts have their email normalized twice (once for the lookup, again inside `remember`).
The benchmark was not kept, so no automated test guards against a performance regression.
b_issues: The added timing test (`< 1_000` ms on 50k+30k contacts) can fail on slow or loaded CI machines.
The timing test also slows the suite by generating 80k contact objects on every run.

verdict.rationale: Both changes swap the linear `findIndex` scan for a normalized-email Map that keeps the first position, so behavior is preserved, and both add a test for the duplicate-existing-entries case. A adds a wall-clock test (under 1 s for 50k+30k) to the suite; it can fail at random on slow CI and its report admits this. B leaves timing out of the suite, benchmarked in a throwaway script, and confirmed its new test passes against the old code. A's code reads a little more clearly, but B's suite is more reliable.
a_issues: Adds a wall-clock timing test (`< 1_000` ms) that can fail at random on slow or loaded CI machines and makes every test run slower.
b_issues: `remember(contact.email, result.push(contact) - 1)` is a bit terse; using the push return value as an index is easy to misread.
New contacts have their email normalized twice (once for the lookup, again inside `remember`), a minor redundancy.
